title: Arakhin 10 - Why Not Sing Hallel on Purim, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kipur?

chapters.title: Minimum and maximum trumpet blasts in the Bet HaMikdash
Musical instruments and flute playing for Halel
Sages' opinions on flute players and the trumpet blast debate
Spacing between blasts and the days for playing flutes
Days when an individual says full Halel
Why Halel is omitted on Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Purim
Ancient instruments from the time of Moshe Rabbenu

summary: Rabbi Hidary goes through Masechet Arakhin, Daf Yod, examining the laws of musical instruments used in the Bet HaMikdash, including silver trumpets, lyres, and reed flutes. The class explores the exact number of trumpet blasts required on various days, the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbanan regarding counting these blasts, and the specific days of the year when Hallel is accompanied by flutes. Finally, the discussion covers why Hallel is not said on certain days like Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Purim, alongside historical details of musical instruments from the time of Moshe Rabbe
questions: How many trumpet blasts were blown in the Bet HaMikdash on a regular day versus a maximum day?
Why do we play flutes alongside Hallel on specific days in the Bet HaMikdash?
What is the difference in opinion between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbanan regarding counting trumpet blasts?
Why is full Hallel not said on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur?
What are the reasons given for why Hallel is not recited on Purim?
